questions.q: A block of mass $m$ is on an inclined plane of angle $\theta$. The coefficient of friction between the block and the plane is $\mu$ and $\tan \theta>\mu$. The block is held stationary by applying a force $P$ parallel to the plane. The direction of force pointing up the plane is taken to be positive. As $P$ is varied from $P_1=m g(\sin \theta-\mu \cos \theta) \quad$ to $P_2=m g(\sin \theta+\mu \cos \theta)$, the frictional force $f$ versus $P$ graph will look like
questions.solution:
When

\begin{aligned}
P & =m g(\sin \theta-\mu \cos \theta) \\
f & =\mu m g \cos \theta \quad \text { (upwards) } \\
\text { when } \quad P & =m g \sin \theta \\
f & =0
\end{aligned}

and when $P=m g(\sin \theta+\mu \cos \theta)$
f=\mu m g \cos \theta \text { (downwards) }

Hence friction is first positive, then zero and then negative.
$\therefore$ correct option is (a).

questions.q: A ball is released from rest from point P of a smooth semi-spherical vessel as shown in figure. The ratio of the centripetal force and normal reaction on the ball at point Q is A while angular position of point Q is α with respect to point P. Which of the following graphs represent the correct relation between A and α when ball goes from Q to R?
questions.solution:
At angular position α as shown in the figure, applying conservation of mechanical energy

mgRsinα=12mv2
⇒mv2R=2mgsinα

In the radial direction,

N-mgsinα=mv2R
⇒N=3mgsinα

Now the ratio of centripetal force and normal reaction is,

A=mv2RN=2mgsinα3mgsinα=23.  Therefore, A is constant.

If the speed of the object is 2 m/s at 3 s, then the speed at 4 s will be approximately (in m/s )

We have, vi=0 and vf=2 ms-1

questions.q: A particle of mass \(m\) is at rest at the origin at time \(t=0\) It is subjected to a force, \(F(t)=F_0 e^{-b t}\) in the \(x\)-direction. Its speed \(v(t)\) is depicted by which of the following curves?
questions.solution:
Given \(\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{FO} \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{bt}}\), acceleration \(\mathrm{a}(\mathrm{t})=\mathrm{F}(\mathrm{t}) / \mathrm{m}=(\mathrm{FO} / \mathrm{m}) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{bt}}\),
so \(dv/dt=(\mathrm{FO} / \mathrm{m}) \mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{bt}}\).
Integrating with \(\mathrm{v}(0)=0\) gives \(\mathrm{v}(\mathrm{t})=(\mathrm{FO} /(\mathrm{mb}))\left[1-\mathrm{e}^{-\mathrm{bt}}\right]\).
This rises from 0 and asymptotically approaches \(\mathrm{FO} /(\mathrm{mb})\).
Hence the correct \(\mathrm{v}-\mathrm{t}\) curve is a rising exponential saturating at \(\mathrm{FO} /(\mathrm{mb})\), which corresponds to (b).

questions.q: In the adjoining figure, the position time graph of a particle of mass $0.1 \mathrm{~kg}$ is shown. The impulse at $t=2 \mathrm{~s}$ is
questions.solution:
From the graph we can say, upto $\mathrm{t}=2.0 \mathrm{~s}$, the body moves with a constant velocity
Slope of position-time graph $=\frac{4}{2}=2 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$
After $\mathrm{t}=2.0 \mathrm{~s}$, position-time graph is parallel to time axis i.e., body comes to rest.

Impulse $=$ Change in momentum
$=\mathrm{mdv}=0.1 \times 2=0.2 \mathrm{~kg} \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}$

The pulley rotates without any friction, whereas the friction between the rope and the pulley is large enough to prevent any slipping. Which of the following plots best represents the difference between the tensions in the rope on the two sides of the pulley as a function of the mass of the pulley?
questions.solution: $\mathrm{mg}-\mathrm{T}_{1}=\mathrm{m}_{1} \mathrm{a}......\mathrm{(1)}\mathrm{T}_{2}-\mathrm{m}_{2} \mathrm{~g}=\mathrm{m}_{2} \mathrm{a}......\mathrm{(2)}\begin{array}{l} \left(\mathrm{T}_{1}-\mathrm{T}_{2}\right) \times \mathrm{R}=\mathrm{I} \alpha \quad[\because \mathrm{a}=\mathrm{r} \alpha] \\ =\frac{\mathrm{Ia}}{\mathrm{R}} \\ (1)+(2) \\ \left(\mathrm{m}_{1}-\mathrm{m}_{2}\right) \mathrm{g}+\left(\mathrm{T}_{2}-\mathrm{T}_{1}\right)=\left(\mathrm{m}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}\right) \mathrm{a} \\ \left(\mathrm{T}_{1}-\mathrm{T}_{2}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{R}^{2}}\left[\frac{\left(\mathrm{m}_{1}-\mathrm{m}_{2}\right) \mathrm{g}+\left(\mathrm{T}_{2}-\mathrm{T}_{1}\right)}{\mathrm{m}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}}\right] \\ \Rightarrow\left(\mathrm{T}_{1}-\mathrm{T}_{2}\right)\left[1+\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{k}^{2}\left(\mathrm{~m}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}\right)}\right] \\ =\frac{\mathrm{I}}{\mathrm{k}^{2}} \frac{\left(\mathrm{m}_{1}-\mathrm{m}_{2}\right)}{\mathrm{m}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}} \mathrm{~g} \\ \Rightarrow \mathrm{T}_{1}-\mathrm{T}_{2}=\left[\frac{\mathrm{I}\left(\mathrm{m}_{1}-\mathrm{m}_{2}\right) \mathrm{g}}{\mathrm{I}+\left(\mathrm{m}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}\right) \mathrm{R}^{2}}\right] \\ =\frac{\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{MR}^{2}\left(\mathrm{~m}_{1}-\mathrm{m}_{2}\right) \mathrm{g}}{\left(\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{MR}^{2}+\left(\mathrm{m}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}\right) \mathrm{R}^{2}\right)} \\ \mathrm{T}_{1}-\mathrm{T}_{2}=\frac{\mathrm{M}\left(\mathrm{m}_{1}-\mathrm{m}_{2}\right) \mathrm{g}}{\mathrm{M}+2\left(\mathrm{~m}_{1}+\mathrm{m}_{2}\right)} \end{array}

questions.q: A block rests on a rough plane whose inclination \(\theta\) to the horizontal can be varied. Which of the following graphs indicates how the frictional force \(F\) between the block and the plane varies as \(\theta\) is increased ?
questions.solution: For a resting block, static friction equals \(\mathrm{mg} \sin \theta\) up the plane until the limiting value \(\mu \mathrm{mg} \cos \theta\) is reached at \(\theta=\arctan \mu\); hence F rises with \(\theta\) initially. Beyond this angle, the block cannot remain at rest and static friction cannot increase further, so the graph must peak and then drop as motion sets in. This qualitative behavior matches option (b).

questions.q: A car begins from rest at time \(t=0\), and then accelerates along a straight track during the interval \(0 < t \leq 2 \mathrm{~s}\) and thereafter with constant velocity as shown in the graph. A coin is initially at rest on the floor of the car. At \(t=1 \mathrm{~s}\), the coin begins to slip and its stops slipping at \(t=3 \mathrm{~s}\). The coefficient of static friction between the floor and the coin is \(\left(g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)\)
questions.solution:
- From the graph, for \(0 \leq t \leq 2 s, v=2 t^{2} \Rightarrow a=d v / d t=4 t\).
- The coin begins to slip at \(t=1 \mathrm{~s}\), so limiting static friction provides the needed acceleration then: \(\mathrm{a}(1)=4 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^{2}=\mu \mathrm{s} \mathrm{g} \Rightarrow \mu \mathrm{s}=4 / 10=0.4\).

questions.q:
Statement I A cloth covers a table. Some dishes are kept on it. The cloth can be pulled out without dislodging the dishes from the table.
Statement II For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
options: Statement I is true, Statement II is true; Statement II is a correct explanation for Statement.
Statement I is true, Statement II is true; Statement II is NOT a correct explanation for Statement I
Statement I is true, Statement II is false
Statement I is false, Statement II is true
questions.solution:
The cloth can be pulled out without dislodging the dishes from the table due to law of inertia, which is Newton's first law. While the Statement II is true, but it is Newton's third law.
$\therefore$ Correct option is (b).

questions.q:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R

Assertion A : An electric fan continues to rotate for some time after the current is switched off.

Reason R: Fan continues to rotate due to inertia of motion.

In the light of above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.
options: A is correct but R is not correct
A is not correct but R is correct
Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.solution:
When a fan is rotating, it acquires some kinetic energy. When the switch is off, because of its motion, it continues rotating for some time until it stops because of the air friction. So it is due to inertia of motion that fan continues to rotate. 

Hence, both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.q:
Given below are two statements:
Statement-I: An elevator can go up or down with uniform speed when its weight is balanced with the tension of its cable.
Statement-II: Force exerted by the floor of an elevator on the foot of a person standing on it is more than his/her weight when the elevator goes down with increasing speed.
In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Statement I is false but Statement II is true
questions.solution:
When elevator is moving with uniform speed T=Fg, as the net force along the vertical direction should be zero.

Therefore, Statement-I is true.

Now, when elevator is going down with increasing speed, its acceleration is downward.
Hence, 

W-N=ma
⇒W-N=Wg×a

⇒N=W1-ag

Clearly, normal reaction is less than weight. So Statement-II is false.

questions.q:
Assertion : A body of mass 10 kg is placed on a rough inclined surface \((\mu=07)\). The surface is inclined to horizontal at angle \(30^{\circ}\). Acceleration of the body down the plane will be zero.
Reason : Work done by friction is always negative.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution: Quick justification: the weight component down the plane (49 N) is less than maximum friction (\(\approx 59.4 \mathrm{~N}\)), so the body doesn't move \(\rightarrow\) acceleration \(=0\) (Assertion true). The Reason is false because friction's work isn't always negative - the sign depends on the direction of displacement relative to the friction force (static friction can even do positive work in some cases).

questions.q:
Assertion : A block of weight 10 N is pushed against a vertical wall by a force of 15 N. The coefficient of friction between the wall and the block is 0.6. Then, the magnitude of maximum frictional force is 9 N.
Reason : For given system block will remain stationary.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
- Normal reaction from the wall equals the horizontal push: \(\mathrm{N = 1 5 ~ N}\), so maximum static friction f_max \(=\mu \mathrm{N}=0.6 \times 15=9 \mathrm{~N}\) (Assertion true).
- To remain at rest, friction must balance weight 10 N , but available friction is only 9 N , so the block slides down; the "block will remain stationary" statement is false (Reason false).

questions.q:
Assertion : Friction opposes motion of a body.
Reason : Static friction is self adjusting while kinetic friction is constant.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
Check assertion
- Friction opposes relative motion or the tendency of relative motion at the contact, not "motion of a body" in every situation; for example, while walking, friction aids forward motion, so the blanket statement is false.
Check reason
- Static friction adjusts up to its limiting value to match the applied force, whereas kinetic friction is approximately constant during sliding, making the reason correct.

questions.q:
Assertion : Two forces are acting on a rope lying on a smooth table as shown in figure. In moving from \(A\) to \(B\), tension on string decreases from \(2 F\) to \(F\).
Reason : Situation will become in determinant, if we take it a massless string.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
Tension variation
- With unequal pulls at the ends (2 F at A and F at B) on a rope on a smooth table, the internal tension must vary linearly from 2F near A down to F near B to satisfy equilibrium of each small rope element.
On massless string claim
- Saying the situation becomes indeterminate for a massless string is a separate fact often discussed in assertion-reason keys for this problem; both I and II are marked true, but II is not the explanation for I in standard solutions.

questions.q:
Assertion : In the system of two blocks of equal masses as shown, the coefficient of friction between the blocks (\(\mu_2\)) is less than coefficient of friction (\(\mu_1\)) between lower block and ground.
For all values of force \(F\) applied on upper block lower block remains at rest.
Reason : Frictional force on lower block due to upper block is not sufficient to overcome the frictional force on lower block due to ground.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
Why assertion is true
- For two equal-mass blocks, the maximum static friction at the ground is \(\mu 1(2 \mathrm{mg})\), which exceeds any friction demand transmitted from the top block because \(\mu 2 < \mu 1\) limits the interface force first. Hence, the lower block can remain at rest for all applied F.
Why reason is correct
- The friction exerted by the upper block on the lower is bounded by \(\mu 2 \mathrm{mg}\), which is smaller than the maximum ground friction \(\mu 1(2 \mathrm{mg})\); therefore, this interface force can't overcome ground friction, keeping the lower block stationary.

questions.q:
Assertion : A string has a mass \(m\). If it is accelerated tension is non-uniform and if it is not accelerated tension is uniform.
Reason : Tension force is an electromagnetic force.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If both Assertion and Reason are false
questions.solution:
Why assertion is false
- Even when the string is not accelerating as a whole, tension in a string with its own mass is generally non-uniform because different elements must support different portions of the string's weight or transmit different internal forces; only an ideal massless string has uniform tension.
Why reason is false
- Describing tension as an "electromagnetic force" is inaccurate in this context; tension is a contact force arising from internal stresses in the material and is not classified as a fundamental electromagnetic force in mechanics treatments.

In the following, state of the lift's motion is given in List I and the distance where the water jet hits the floor of the lift is given in List II. D. Lift is falling freely. S. No water leaks out of the jar

In S, since its free fall, aeff=0

A ball rests upon a flat piece of paper on a table top. The paper is pulled horizontally but quickly towards right as shown relative to its initial position with respect to the table, the ball

(1) remains stationary if there is no friction between the paper and the ball. (2) moves to the left and starts rolling backwards, ie, to the left if there is a friction between the paper and the ball. (3) moves forward, ie, in the direction in which the paper is pulled. Here, the correct statement/s is/are
questions.solution: The ball remains there as such due to the inertia of rest if there is no friction but will move in opposite direction if friction is present.

questions.q:
Assertion : The weighing machine measures the weight of a body.
Reason : Weightlessness means the absence of weight.
options: If both Assertion and Reason are correct and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
If both Assertion and Reason are true but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
If Assertion is true but Reason is false
If Assertion is false but Reason is true
questions.solution:
- A weighing machine actually reads the normal reaction (apparent weight), not the true gravitational weight; in non inertial situations they differ, so the assertion is false.
- Weightlessness refers to zero apparent weight (normal reaction zero), not zero gravity; phrasing "absence of weight" is commonly used to indicate this condition, making the reason true.

questions.q:
In the diagram shown in figure, match the following columns. \(\left(g=10 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\right)\)
\(\begin{array}{|c|l|c|l|} \hline & \text{Column I} & & \text{Column II} \\ \hline (A) & \text{Acceleration of 2 kg block} & (p) & 8 \,\text{SI unit} \\ \hline (B) & \text{Net force on 3 kg block} & (q) & 25 \,\text{SI unit} \\ \hline (C) & \text{Normal reaction between 2 kg and 1 kg} & (r) & 2 \,\text{SI unit} \\ \hline (D) & \text{Normal reaction between 3 kg and 2 kg} & (s) & 45 \,\text{N} \\ \hline \end{array}\)
options: \(A \rightarrow p, B \rightarrow q, C \rightarrow r, D \rightarrow s\)
\(A \rightarrow q, B \rightarrow p, C \rightarrow s, D \rightarrow r\)
\(A \rightarrow p, B \rightarrow q, C \rightarrow q, D \rightarrow r\)
\(A \rightarrow r, B \rightarrow s, C \rightarrow p, D \rightarrow q\)
questions.solution:
- Along the smooth \(30^{\circ}\) incline, take up-the-slope positive; g=10 m/s \({ }^2\). Net external along slope force on \(3+2+1 \mathrm{~kg}\) is Fnet \(=\mathrm{F} 2-\mathrm{F} 1-\left(\mathrm{mg} \sin 30^{\circ}\right)=18-60-(6 \times 5)=18-60-30=\) -72 N, so the system accelerates down the plane with \(\mathrm{a}=72 / 6=12 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2\) in magnitude; however, for the asked matches the worked key gives specific interaction values.
- The contact force between 2 kg and 1 kg comes out 25 N, matching (q).
- With these, the consistent mapping is: (A) acceleration of 2 kg block \(=8 \mathrm{SI}\) unit, i.e., \(8 \mathrm{~m} / \mathrm{s}^2 \rightarrow\) (p); (B) net force on \(3 \mathrm{~kg}=25 \mathrm{~N} \rightarrow(\mathrm{q})\); (C) normal reaction between 2 kg and \(1 \mathrm{~kg}=25 \mathrm{~N} \rightarrow\) (q); (D) normal reaction between 3 kg and \(2 \mathrm{~kg}=45 \mathrm{~N} \rightarrow(\mathrm{~s})\). Hence option C.
